title: Other points of view: what someone else sees, knows and needs

summary.text: Two people at one table never see the same table. What you see depends on where you sit, and what you think depends on what you know. Children of three and four can already work out what another person sees, though scientists once thought this came only at about seven. In this unit you draw what someone across the table sees, test which eye each person in your family sees with first, and play games where you think like someone else. People and their bodies differ in many hidden ways, and friends who know this can share, take turns and work well together.
summary.art: A dining table seen from above with a steel tumbler, a banana and a lime on it, and two children sitting on opposite sides, each with a dotted line from their eyes showing a different view.

intro.hook: Sit at the dining table and put a steel tumbler in the middle. Hide a lime behind it, so you cannot see the lime. Can the person sitting opposite you see it? How do you know, without getting up?
intro.text: Everyone looks at the world from their own place. A tumbler that hides a lime from you may show it plainly to someone else. People also know different things, so they can think different things about the same box or the same quarrel. In this unit you test how well you can picture another person's view. You find hidden differences inside your own family. You learn what scientists found about how children come to understand other minds, and why friends who see things differently can still do things well together.
intro.art: A child sitting at a table, peering round a steel tumbler at a lime behind it, while a grandmother on the far side can see the lime clearly.

outcomes: I can draw what another person sees from a different seat, and check my drawing against a photo from that seat.
I can explain that what a person thinks depends on what they have seen and been told, so two people can believe different things about the same thing.
I can name some hidden ways people's bodies differ, such as the hand they write with, the eye they look with first, and how they see colours.
I can tell how Jean Piaget and Bärbel Inhelder thought young children could not picture another person's view, and how Martin Hughes's hiding game showed they could.
I can tell a quarrel or a story from the other person's side, and say what they saw and wanted.
I can plan a game or a job so that people with different bodies, skills and ideas can all take part.

terms.meaning: The place a person sees from, or the way they think about something because of what they know and feel.
terms.example: From your chair the tumbler hides the lime. From Amma's chair the lime is in plain view. You have different points of view.
terms.art: Two eyes drawn at two sides of a table, each with a cone of lines showing what they see.

terms.meaning: Picturing what another person sees, knows or feels from where they are.
terms.example: Before you hold up your drawing, you turn it round so your friend can see it the right way up. You took her perspective.
terms.art: A child turning a drawing round to face a friend across a table.

terms.meaning: What a person thinks is true. A belief can be right or wrong.
terms.example: Paati thinks the biscuit tin holds biscuits. If someone filled it with buttons, her belief is wrong, though it made good sense.
terms.art: A grandmother looking at a closed biscuit tin with a thought bubble showing biscuits.

terms.meaning: A belief that is wrong because the person has not seen or heard what changed.
terms.example: Your brother saw the ball go into the cupboard. While he was out, you moved it under the bed. He still thinks it is in the cupboard.
terms.art: A boy pointing to a cupboard while the ball he wants is under a bed behind him.

terms.meaning: Knowing that other people have their own thoughts, wishes and beliefs, which can be different from yours.
terms.example: You know your friend wants the red crayon, even though you like the blue one best.
terms.art: Two children, each with a thought bubble holding a different crayon.

terms.meaning: Working together to reach a goal that you could not reach as well alone.
terms.example: One person holds the paper flat while the other draws the kolam. Together the lines come out straight.
terms.art: Two children on a floor, one holding a sheet of paper flat while the other draws a kolam pattern.

terms.meaning: The eye your brain uses first when you line up or aim at something. Most people have one.
terms.example: When you look through a keyhole, you put one eye to it without thinking. That is often your dominant eye.
terms.art: A child looking through a small hole in a sheet of paper at a wall clock, with one eye closed.

terms.meaning: Seeing some colours differently from most people, because some of the light-sensing cells in the eye work differently.
terms.example: Many people with red-green colour blindness find it hard to tell a red chilli from a green one by colour alone.
terms.art: A red chilli and a green chilli side by side, and next to them the same two drawn in two similar brownish shades.

terms.meaning: Using the left hand more, and with more skill, for jobs like writing and throwing.
terms.example: About 1 person in 10 writes with their left hand.
terms.art: A girl writing in a notebook with her left hand.

explanations.concept: What a point of view is
explanations.definition: A point of view is the place a person sees from. It also means the way they think about something, because of what they know.
explanations.description: Light travels in straight lines. So from each place, some things are in view and some are hidden behind others. Two people at one table see two different pictures, and both are true. The same is true for thinking. A person who has seen the box being opened knows what is inside. A person who has not seen it can only guess from the outside.
examples: From the front seat of an auto you can see the road ahead. From the back seat you mostly see the driver's back.
A teacher at the blackboard sees every child's face. Each child sees the blackboard and the backs of other heads.
Your grandmother remembers your street before the flats were built. You only know it as it is now.
explanations.art: An auto-rickshaw from the side, with the view from the front seat and the view from the back seat shown in two small boxes.
explanations.context: This card is about what a point of view means, for seeing and for thinking.

explanations.definition: Visual perspective taking is working out what another person can see from where they are.
explanations.description: There are two steps. The first is knowing whether a thing is in someone's view at all. Children of two or three can already do this. They know that a toy behind a wall is hidden from someone on the other side. The second step is working out how a thing looks from there: what is on their left, what is in front. This is harder, and it keeps getting better through primary school. Left and right are the hardest part, because they swap when someone faces you.
examples: A three-year-old playing hide and seek knows to hide behind the curtain, not in front of it.
When you face someone, your right hand is on the same side as their left hand.
Map readers turn the map round so that it points the way they are facing.
explanations.art: Two children facing each other across a table, each raising their right hand, with arrows showing the hands are on opposite sides of the table.
explanations.context: This card is about the two steps in picturing another person's view. It goes with the Other Chair Test.

explanations.concept: Knowing that others think different things
explanations.definition: Theory of mind is knowing that other people have their own thoughts, wishes and beliefs, which can differ from yours and from the truth.
explanations.description: In 1983, Heinz Wimmer and Josef Perner told children a story. A boy called Maxi puts his chocolate in a cupboard and goes out. His mother moves it. Where will Maxi look when he comes back? Most children of three said he would look where the chocolate really is. Most children of five or six said he would look in the cupboard, where he left it. They understood that Maxi had a false belief. In 1985, Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie and Uta Frith made a shorter version with two dolls, Sally and Anne. It is now used all over the world.
examples: Hide a sweet while your brother is out of the room. You know he will look in the old place.
A magic trick works because the watchers believe something false about where the coin is.
A surprise party works only if the guest of honour believes nothing is happening.
explanations.art: Two dolls on a table, one with a basket and one with a box, and a marble being moved from the basket to the box while the first doll is turned away.
explanations.context: This card is about how children learn that other people can believe things that are not true. It goes with the Biscuit Box Surprise.

explanations.definition: People differ in many ways that you cannot see from outside: in how their senses work, which hand and eye they use first, and what they find easy or hard.
explanations.description: About 1 person in 10 is left-handed. Most people have one eye that the brain uses first for aiming, and for about two people in three it is the right eye. Some people see colours differently. In many countries about 1 boy or man in 12 has some red-green colour blindness, and about 1 girl or woman in 200. The numbers vary from place to place. Many people do not find this out until they are tested. So two people looking at one thing may not receive the same picture of it.
examples: A left-handed child bumps elbows with a right-handed child if they sit on the wrong sides at a table.
A cricket player may hold the bat one way and write with the other hand.
A colour-blind child may find a map that uses only red and green hard to read.
explanations.art: A row of five children from one class: one writing left-handed, one squinting through a paper hole with the left eye, one looking at a red and green map with a puzzled face.
explanations.context: This card is about the hidden ways bodies differ. It goes with the Dominant Eye Test.

explanations.description: Scientists who study children have no single agreed definition of a friend. But they find that friends choose to spend time together, share, help each other and trust each other. Young children often call someone a friend because they play together. Older children add that a friend understands you and keeps your secrets. Friends quarrel too. Studies find that friends are more likely than other children to talk a quarrel through and stay together after it. Understanding your friend's point of view helps you do that.
examples: Two friends at the park take turns on the swing without being told.
A friend notices you are quiet and asks if you are all right.
After a quarrel over a game, two friends agree on a new rule and play again.
explanations.art: Two girls in school uniform sharing one umbrella in the rain on the way home.
explanations.context: This card is about what scientists find friends do for each other.

explanations.description: In 1971, schools in Austin, in the United States, had just mixed children from different backgrounds, and there were fights in class. A psychologist called Elliot Aronson and his students tried a new way of teaching. Each child in a small group got one piece of a lesson, and only the whole group together had all of it. Each child needed the others. In his studies, children in these groups came to like each other more than children taught the usual way. This is now called the jigsaw classroom. Scientists still argue about when meeting and working with different people helps them get on, and when it does not.
examples: A cooking team where one person reads the recipe, one measures and one stirs.
A cricket team needs batters, bowlers and a wicketkeeper, who all do different jobs.
A street that celebrates Onam, Eid and Christmas together, each family cooking for the others.

perspectives.who: Gordon Allport, a psychologist, in 1954, and many who followed him
perspectives.explanation: Meeting people from another group helps people get on, most of all when they are equals, work towards the same goal, and the grown-ups around them support it.
Just being near each other is not enough. If people compete, or meet only once, they may get on worse. The way they meet matters more than meeting.

explanations.art: Four children round a table, each holding one piece of a jigsaw map, fitting them together in the middle.
explanations.context: This card is about what helps different people get on, and where scientists disagree.

explanations.concept: Do animals know what others see?
explanations.description: In 2000, Brian Hare, Josep Call and Michael Tomasello put two pieces of food in a room with two chimpanzees, one high-ranking and one low-ranking. The high-ranking chimp usually takes any food they can see. One piece of food was hidden from the high-ranking chimp by a screen, and the other was in their view. The low-ranking chimp mostly went for the hidden piece. So the low-ranking chimp seemed to know what the other could see.
examples: A low-ranking chimp went for food that the high-ranking chimp could not see.
A dog often waits until you look away before taking food off a plate.
A crow at the window may fly off as soon as you look straight at them.

perspectives.who: Brian Hare, Michael Tomasello and many others
perspectives.explanation: Chimpanzees know what another chimp can and cannot see, and use it to decide what to do.
The chimp may be following a simple rule, such as 'go for food behind a screen'. We cannot yet be sure they picture another's view.

explanations.art: Two chimpanzees in a room with two bananas, one banana hidden from the bigger chimp by a screen, and the smaller chimp reaching for that one.
explanations.context: This card is about whether animals can tell what others see.

agreed.text: Even children of two or three know when a thing is hidden from another person.
agreed.evidence: In hiding games with dolls and walls, such as Martin Hughes's study in 1975, most children of three and four hid a doll where a 'policeman' doll could not see them.

agreed.text: Most children understand that someone can hold a false belief by about four or five years old.
agreed.evidence: In false-belief tests like Maxi and the chocolate, and Sally and Anne, most children of three fail and most children of five pass, in many countries.

agreed.text: People's bodies and senses differ in ways you cannot see from outside.
agreed.evidence: Simple tests show that people differ in their writing hand, their dominant eye and how they see colours.

challenging.claim: Children under about seven cannot picture what another person sees.
challenging.who: Jean Piaget and Bärbel Inhelder, from their three mountains task in the 1940s
challenging.for: In their task, many young children picked the picture of their own view when asked what a doll on the other side could see.
challenging.against: In tasks that made sense to children, such as hiding a doll from a policeman doll, most children of three and four got it right. The mountains task was hard for other reasons: choosing between pictures of mountains.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea about young children, and how it was tested.

challenging.claim: Opposites attract, so we choose friends who are very different from us.
challenging.for: Friends with different skills can help each other, and some friends really are very different.
challenging.against: Many studies find that people, children too, more often make friends with people who are like them in age, interests and habits.
challenging.context: This card is about a saying about friends, and what studies find.

challenging.claim: Only humans can tell what another being can see.
challenging.for: Humans can talk about what others see and think, and no other animal can tell us.
challenging.against: In tests, chimpanzees go for food that a stronger chimp cannot see, and scrub jays move hidden food when another jay has watched them hide it.
challenging.context: This card is about whether seeing from another's point of view is only human.

big_questions.q: You and Amma saw two different pictures of the same table. Which picture was the real table?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether any one seat can see every side at once.

big_questions.q: You are not inside your friend's body. So how can you know what they need?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you can learn by watching, by asking, and by remembering a time you felt the same.

big_questions.q: A colour-blind child and you look at one chilli. Are you seeing the same chilli differently, or seeing different chillies?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the colour is: in the chilli, in the light, or in the eye and the brain.

big_questions.q: Would the world be better if everyone thought the same way?
big_questions.hint: Think about a cooking team or a cricket team where everyone does the same job.

big_questions.q: A crow, an ant and you are on the same balcony. Whose view of the balcony is the right one?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each of them notices and needs there.

story.title: The Monster Under Meenu's Cot
story.note: The story is made up, from a story seed in the founder's notebook. What it shows is true: a thing looks very different from another place, and a person can only know what they have seen or been told.
text: Meenu was seven, and she lived with her Appa and her Paati in a small flat in Madurai. Every night Appa read her a story. Then he looked under her cot, said "No monsters," and switched off the light.

One night, after Appa had gone, Meenu heard a scratching sound. It came from under the cot. She pulled the sheet up to her nose. In the light from the street, two pointed shadows rose on the wall. They looked like horns.
"Go away!" Meenu said, as loudly as she dared.
"Please don't shout," said a small, shaky voice. "Your voice is like thunder down here."
A creature crept out and sat on the floor. He was about as big as a cat. He had two curly horns, long claws and big round eyes. He was trembling.
"You have horns and claws," said Meenu. "You look scary."
"These are just how I look," said the monster. "I use my claws to climb, and my horns have never hurt anyone. My name is Kombu. I came in through the window to get out of the rain."
"Then why were you scratching?" asked Meenu.
"I was trying to dig a dry corner in your old blanket," said Kombu. "I didn't know you were awake. And you look scary too, you know."
Meenu sat up. "Me? I'm small."
"Not from down here," said Kombu. "Come and see."
Meenu thought about it. Then she climbed down and lay flat on the floor next to Kombu, with her cheek on the cool tiles. She looked up.

The cot was like a roof over a dark cave. Her own chappals by the door looked as big as boats. When Paati coughed in the next room, the sound boomed through the floor. Meenu's school bag stood against the wall like a tall brown hill. She could not see her bed, her books or her window at all.
"Oh," said Meenu. "From here, everything is huge. And I can't see anything up high."
"That is my whole world," said Kombu. "Feet, chappals and dust. When you stamp, the floor shakes. When you shout, my ears hurt."
Meenu thought for a while. "And from up on my cot, I only saw two horn shadows on the wall. I didn't see your eyes. I didn't see you shaking."
"The shadows were bigger than me," said Kombu. "The street light was behind me and the wall was far away."
"So I saw a big shadow, and you saw a big girl," said Meenu. "We were both scared of something that wasn't true."
Kombu nodded so hard his horns wobbled.

Meenu had an idea. She went to her cupboard and took out an old cotton towel. She folded it into a soft square and put it in the dry corner under the cot. "You can sleep here tonight," she said. "But you have to tell me what you need, because I can't see it from up there."
"I need quiet," said Kombu. "And no stamping. And maybe one idli in the morning."
"I need you not to scratch," said Meenu. "And not to make horn shadows on my wall."
Kombu moved into the corner, away from the street light. The horn shadows vanished.

In the morning Paati found Meenu asleep on the floor beside the cot. Meenu woke and looked under it. The towel was there, folded neatly, but Kombu had gone. On the window ledge sat a single dry leaf, which had not been there the night before.
At breakfast Meenu saved one idli on a small steel plate by the window. Paati raised her eyebrows.
"It is for a friend," said Meenu. "He sees the world from very low down."
"Ah," said Paati, as if that made perfect sense. "Then put the plate on the floor, kanna. He might not reach the ledge."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenu and Kombu were each frightened by what they saw from their own place. From the cot, the street light behind Kombu threw a big horn shadow on the wall. From the floor, a girl looks huge and her voice is loud. Neither could see the other's view until Meenu lay down where Kombu lived. Then she asked him what he needed, because some things you cannot see even from another place: you have to be told.
ask: Why did Kombu's shadow look so much bigger than Kombu?
What did Meenu see when she lay on the floor that she could not see from her cot?
Why was Kombu scared of Meenu?
Meenu said, "You have to tell me what you need." Why couldn't she just look and see?
Paati told Meenu to put the plate on the floor. Whose point of view was Paati thinking from?

games.title: Guess Who I Am: answer as someone else
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each player secretly becomes someone else, and answers questions as that person or animal would. The others guess who it is.

printables.title: 24 'I am' cards to cut out
items: a cricket player waiting to bat
a girl on her first day at a new school
a cat sitting on a wall
an ant on the kitchen floor
a dog left alone at home
a vegetable seller on a hot afternoon
a child who is colour blind looking at a painting
a left-handed child at a crowded table
a doctor in a busy hospital
a traffic police officer at a busy signal
a girl who just moved from Kolkata to Hyderabad
a tourist who speaks no Tamil in Madurai

printables.title: 12 question cards
items: What can you see right now?
What do you want most today?
What sound do you hear the most?
Who looks after you, or who do you look after?
What would make your day better?
What do you know that most people don't?
What is hard for you that is easy for others?
What do big people or big things look like to you?

rules: Shuffle the 'I am' cards and put them face down. Put the question cards face down in another pile.
On your turn, take an 'I am' card without showing anyone. You are now that person or animal.
The other players take turns to read a question card to you. You answer as the one on your card, from their point of view. You must not say what you are.
After each answer, any player may make one guess. A right guess scores 1 point for the guesser and 1 point for you.
If nobody guesses after five questions, show your card, and nobody scores.
Play until everyone has had two turns. Playing with one grown-up, take turns and count how many questions each guess needed.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Read the rules together. 3. Play one practice turn where the grown-up is 'a crow at a window'.
flow.say: I am going to be someone secret. Ask me a question card, and I will answer the way they would. Ready? 'What can you see right now?' I see a girl eating a dosa, and I want the last piece.
flow.kid: Amma is someone secret. Ask her a question. Who is she?
flow.context: This is the first step of Guess Who I Am, a game where you answer questions as someone else.

flow.do: Play the game. Each player takes two turns.
flow.say: Answer from inside their life. Not what you would say, but what they would say.
flow.kid: Take a card. Be that one. Answer like them.
flow.parent: If a child answers as themselves ('I like ice cream') for a crow, ask, 'Would a crow say that? What does a crow want?' Answers that show a real point of view, such as an ant saying 'Feet are like falling buildings', are the best part of the game.

check.q: Your card says 'a baby of one year'. Someone asks 'What do big people look like to you?' Which answer is from the baby's point of view?
options: Like giants, and I mostly see their knees
Like friends who help with my homework
Like players in my cricket team
check.why: A baby of one is very small and sees grown-ups from below. A baby does not do homework or play cricket. If you chose one of those, you answered as yourself, not as the baby.

flow.do: Finish and talk about the game.
flow.say: Whose card was the hardest to be? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was hardest to be? Why?
flow.think: Can you ever know for sure what a crow sees and wants?

experiments.title: The Other Chair Test: can you draw what someone else sees?
experiments.question: Sitting in your own chair, can you draw what a person in another chair sees on the table?
experiments.predict: Before you draw, guess. Will the person opposite see the lime? Will the banana be on their left or their right? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep the three things in exactly the same places all through the test. Draw each view while sitting in your own chair, without getting up or leaning. Check each drawing against a photo taken from that seat at sitting eye height. Only the seat changes.
results_table: My drawing: what is on the left?
Photo: what is on the left?

materials.item: a tall steel tumbler or a steel dabba
a banana
a lime, or any small round thing such as a ball or an onion
a table or a mat on the floor, with room for people on two or three sides
paper and a pencil
a phone with a camera, held by a grown-up. No phone? The child can go and sit in the seat to check instead.

experiments.safety: Nothing in this test is unsafe. A grown-up looks after the phone.

schedule.what: Set out three things on a table. Draw your own view, then guess and draw two other people's views. Check each one with a photo from that seat.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick or draw the photos next to your drawings, and circle anything that came out different.

flow.do: 1. Put the tumbler in the middle of the table. 2. Put the banana to one side of it. 3. Put the lime close behind the tumbler on the far side, so your child cannot see it.
flow.say: This is our table for the test. You can't see the lime from your chair, can you? The tumbler is in the way.
flow.kid: Sit in your chair. Look at the table. Can you see the lime? The tumbler hides it.
flow.parent: Use a tumbler taller than the lime, and put the lime right against it, so it is fully hidden from your child's seat. A grown-up sits opposite the child. The side seat stays empty for now.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Other Chair Test. You set three things on a table so that one is hidden from you.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw just what they see from their own chair. Write 'My seat' on it.
flow.say: Draw only what you can see from where you sit. Not what you know is there. Just what reaches your eyes.
flow.kid: Draw what you see from your chair. Only what you can see.
flow.parent: This first drawing is a warm-up. Many children add the lime because they know it is there. That is fine. Ask, 'Can you see it right now?'

flow.do: 1. Sit opposite your child. 2. Ask them to draw what you see from your chair, without getting up. 3. Ask the two prediction questions and write the answers in the table.
flow.say: Now draw what I can see from my chair. Stay in your seat. Will I see the lime? Will the banana be on my left or my right? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stay in your chair. Draw what Amma sees. Will she see the lime? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think I can see the lime?
good: Because the tumbler is between me and the lime, but not between you and the lime.
Because the lime is on your side.

flow.parent: Don't help or hint. Any guess with a reason is good. Ask them to point to your left hand before they decide about the banana, if they want to.

flow.do: 1. Hold the phone at your own eye height, sitting in your chair. 2. Take a photo of the table. 3. Put the photo next to your child's drawing. 4. Together, tick or cross: the lime, the banana's side, the tumbler.
flow.say: Here is what my chair really sees. Let's put it next to your drawing. What did you get right? What came out different?
flow.kid: Look at the photo from Amma's chair. Is it like your drawing?
flow.parent: Many children get the lime right but put the banana on the wrong side, because left and right swap for someone facing you. Some forget that the banana can hide part of the tumbler from that side. Whatever they find is a real result.

check.q: You sit opposite Amma. The banana is on your right. Where is it for Amma?
check.why: When two people face each other, left and right swap. Your right side of the table is her left side. If you chose 'on her right too', try standing face to face and both pointing to the banana.

flow.do: 1. A second person sits at the side of the table, or you move there. 2. Your child stays in their chair and draws that view. 3. Take a photo from the side seat at sitting eye height. 4. Compare again and fill in the table.
flow.say: Now the side seat. This is harder. From there, what is in front, and what is behind? Is anything hidden?
flow.kid: Now draw the view from the side chair. What is in front?
flow.parent: From the side, the three things may line up differently. The banana may now be in front of the tumbler, or the lime may peep out. Let your child find this from the photo, not from you.

flow.do: Talk about the results. Ask your child to say a claim, the evidence and a reason.
flow.say: Which seat was hardest to draw? What did you get wrong, and why do you think it happened? Was any drawing the true table?
flow.kid: Which seat was hardest? Why? Which drawing was the real table?

ask.q: Which drawing shows the real table?
good: All of them show the real table, from different places.
None shows all of it. You need the photos together to know where everything is.

flow.think: Is there any one place you could sit and see every side of the tumbler at once?

experiments.context: In this experiment you try to draw what a person in another chair sees, then check with a photo from their chair.

experiments.title: The Dominant Eye Test: does everyone at home look with the same eye first?
experiments.question: Does everyone in the family use the same eye first when they aim, and is it on the same side as the hand they write with?
experiments.predict: Guess which eye each person in your family uses first. Will it be on the same side as their writing hand? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everyone looks at the same thing from the same spot, through the same hole, with both eyes open first. Each person does the test three times, because one try can be a mistake.

materials.item: a sheet of paper or a postcard with a hole about the size of a one rupee coin cut in the middle
something small to look at on a far wall, such as a clock or a switch, at least 3 metres away
paper and a pencil for the table
as many family members or neighbours as will join, at least three people

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the hole with scissors.

schedule.what: Find each person's dominant eye three times and their writing hand. Fill in the table and look for a pattern.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then count how many people are right-eyed and how many are left-eyed.

flow.do: 1. Cut a hole about the size of a one rupee coin in the middle of the paper. 2. Choose a small thing on a far wall, such as the clock.
flow.say: We are going to find out which eye each of us uses first. Most people have one, and they don't know which.
flow.kid: Your brain picks one eye to aim with. Which one?
flow.parent: A rough hole is fine. It should be small enough that only the clock shows through it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dominant Eye Test. You make a paper with a hole to find which eye each person aims with.

flow.do: Ask everyone to guess which eye they will use, and why. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Before we test, guess. Which eye do you think you use first? Will it match the hand you write with? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess your eye. Left or right? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Let each person guess. Many people guess it matches their writing hand. This is often true, but not always.

flow.do: 1. Hold the paper at arm's length with both hands. 2. With both eyes open, look through the hole at the clock. 3. Keep still and close the left eye. Is the clock still in the hole? 4. Open it, and close the right eye. 5. The eye that keeps the clock in the hole is the dominant eye. 6. Do it three times for each person.
flow.say: Look through the hole at the clock, with both eyes open. Now close one eye. Did the clock jump out of the hole? Now the other eye.
flow.kid: Look at the clock through the hole. Close one eye. Did it jump?
flow.parent: With one eye the clock stays in the hole. With the other, the clock jumps to the side. If a person gets a different eye each try, write 'not clear'. That happens for some people.

check.q: Lakshmi closes her left eye and the clock stays in the hole. She closes her right eye and the clock jumps away. Which is her dominant eye?
check.why: With only her right eye open, the clock stayed in the hole, so she lined it up with her right eye. If you chose the left eye, look again at which eye was open when the clock stayed.

flow.do: 1. Ask each person which hand they write with. 2. Fill in the table. 3. Count the right-eyed and left-eyed people. 4. Talk about the pattern.
flow.say: Did everyone use the same eye? Did it always match their writing hand? Were you surprised by anyone?
flow.kid: Count the right eyes and left eyes. Any surprises?

ask.q: We all looked at the same clock. Did we all see it with the same eye first?
good: No, some of us used the left eye and some the right.
Yes in our family, but the hand did not always match.

flow.think: If two people don't even aim with the same eye, what else might be different inside them that nobody can see?

experiments.context: In this experiment you find which eye each person in your family uses first, a difference nobody can see from outside.

setup.art: A hand holding a postcard with a coin-sized hole in it at arm's length, with a wall clock visible through the hole.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the clock through the hole, both eyes open.

setup.art: The same view with one eye closed and the clock still in the hole, and a second picture with the other eye closed and the clock jumped to the side.
setup.caption: 2. Close each eye in turn. The eye that keeps the clock in the hole is the dominant one.

activities.title: Hide From the Watchmen: Martin Hughes's hiding game

materials.item: two books stood up and crossed in a plus shape, to make four walls with four corners
two small toys or bottle caps with faces drawn on, to be the watchmen
one tiny toy, an eraser or a coin, to be the one who hides

activities.safety: Nothing in this activity is unsafe.

schedule.what: Hide a small toy from one watchman, then from two. Then swap: the child places the watchmen and the grown-up hides.

activities.record: Draw the walls from above. Mark each watchman with W and where you hid the toy with a star.

flow.do: 1. Stand two books on a table in a plus shape, making four corners. 2. Put one watchman at the end of one wall. 3. Give your child the tiny toy.
flow.say: This watchman is looking for the little one. Hide the little one where the watchman can't see them.
flow.kid: Hide the little toy. The watchman must not see it.
flow.parent: This is the game Martin Hughes played with children of three and four in Edinburgh in 1975. Your child will very likely find it easy. That is the point: even small children can work out what someone else can see.
flow.context: This is a quick hiding game to start the unit. You hide a toy where a toy watchman cannot see it.

flow.do: 1. Add a second watchman at the end of another wall. 2. Ask your child to hide the toy from both. 3. Ask how they know each watchman can't see it.
flow.say: Now there are two watchmen. Find a corner neither of them can see. How do you know?
flow.kid: Two watchmen now. Find a corner neither can see. How do you know?

ask.q: How do you know the watchman can't see that corner?
good: The wall is between the watchman and the corner.
If I put my eye where the watchman is, I can't see it.

flow.parent: Only one corner is hidden from both, if the watchmen stand at the ends of two walls that are next to each other. If your child puts their eye down where the watchman stands to check, that is exactly what scientists do.

flow.do: Swap roles. Your child places the two watchmen, and you try to hide the toy.
flow.say: Your turn to be the boss. Place the watchmen so that it is hard for me to hide.
flow.kid: Your turn. Place the watchmen. Can Amma still hide?
flow.think: How did you know what a toy could see, when a toy has no real eyes?

activities.context: This is a hiding game to start the unit. A child hides a toy from toy watchmen behind book walls.

activities.title: The Biscuit Box Surprise: what will Paati think is inside?

materials.item: an empty biscuit packet box, sweet box or tea box that shows on the outside what it held
something unexpected to put inside it, such as pencils, buttons or clothes pegs
a family member who has not seen you fill the box

activities.safety: Nothing in this activity is unsafe.

schedule.what: Fill a biscuit box with pencils. Guess what someone will say is inside, then ask them. If a child of three or four is nearby, ask them too.

activities.record: Write each person's name, your guess of what they will say, and what they said.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the closed biscuit box. 2. Ask what is inside. 3. Open it and show the pencils. 4. Close it again.
flow.say: What do you think is in this box? Let's look. Oh, pencils! Now, before you opened it, what did you think was inside?
flow.kid: What is in the box? Open it. Were you right?
flow.parent: Put the pencils in before you start, out of sight. Most children say 'biscuits'. Children of three often say afterwards that they thought 'pencils' all along.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Biscuit Box Surprise. A box that looks like biscuits holds pencils.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what Paati, or someone else who has not seen inside, will say is in the box. 2. Ask why. 3. Write the guess.
flow.say: Paati hasn't seen inside. What will she say is in the box? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Paati hasn't looked. What will she say is inside? Why?

ask.q: Why will Paati say biscuits, when you know it is pencils?
good: Because the box looks like a biscuit box, and that is all she knows.

flow.do: 1. Your child shows the closed box to Paati and asks what is inside. 2. Compare with the guess. 3. Is a child of three or four nearby? With their family's agreement, try it with them too. Ask them what they first thought.
flow.say: Was your guess right? Paati believed something that was not true. Why did it make good sense for her to believe it?
flow.kid: Ask Paati. Was your guess right? Why did she think that?
flow.parent: Paati will almost certainly say biscuits, and your child will have predicted it. That shows your child understands a false belief. With a three-year-old the answers are often surprising: many say the next person will say 'pencils', because that is what they now know.

check.q: Farhan, aged 8, puts buttons in a sweet box. His friend Divya has not seen inside. What will Divya say is in the box?
options: Buttons, because that is what is inside
Sweets, because the box looks like a sweet box
check.why: Divya can only go by what she has seen, and she has seen a sweet box. Her belief is false, but it makes sense. If you chose buttons, remember that Divya never saw Farhan put them in.

activities.context: In this activity you find out what someone thinks is inside a box when they have not seen inside. It is a home version of a famous test.

activities.title: Jigsaw Nimbu Paani: one card each, one drink together

materials.item: four instruction cards, written by a grown-up from the steps below, one for each person
a lime, a knife and a board, a jug of drinking water, sugar, salt, a spoon and tumblers

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the lime with the knife.

schedule.what: Make nimbu paani together, where each person holds only one card of the recipe.

activities.record: Write who held which card, and one thing that went wrong and how you fixed it together.

flow.do: 1. Write four cards. Card 1 says: Pour 4 tumblers of water into the jug. Card 2 says: A grown-up cuts the lime, and you squeeze it into the jug. Card 3 says: Add 4 spoons of sugar and a pinch of salt. Card 4 says: Stir until the sugar disappears, then taste and pour. 2. Give one card to each person.
flow.say: Each of us has one part of the recipe. You can read your card out loud, but you can't show it. We can only make the drink if we all work it out together.
flow.kid: You have one card. Read it out. Don't show it.
flow.parent: With fewer than four people, give some people two cards. This is a home version of the jigsaw classroom, where each child holds one piece of a lesson.
flow.context: This is the first step of Jigsaw Nimbu Paani. Each person holds one card of a recipe, and nobody can make the drink alone.

flow.do: Let the family work out the order and make the drink. Step in only to cut the lime.
flow.say: Who goes first? How do we know? Does the sugar go in before or after the water?
flow.kid: Who goes first? Talk about it. Then make the drink.
flow.parent: Let them argue a little about the order. The point is that everyone's card is needed, including the youngest person's.

flow.do: Taste the drink and talk about it.
flow.say: Could anyone have made this alone with just their card? What happened when we didn't agree?
flow.kid: Could you make it alone with your card? Why not?
flow.think: Was the youngest person's card less important than the others?

activities.context: In this activity each person holds one part of a recipe, and the family must work together to make nimbu paani.

activities.title: Tell It From the Other Side: the crocodile's story

materials.item: the Panchatantra story of the monkey and the crocodile, read from a book or told from memory
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Nothing in this activity is unsafe.

schedule.what: Hear the story of the monkey and the crocodile. Then tell it again as the crocodile would tell it.

activities.record: Draw the crocodile in the river and write three things the crocodile saw, wanted or was afraid of.

flow.do: Tell the story briefly. A monkey lives in a jamun tree by a river and gives jamun fruit to a crocodile. The crocodile's wife wants the monkey's heart. The crocodile carries the monkey into the river to trick him. The monkey escapes by saying he left his heart in the tree.
flow.say: This is an old story from the Panchatantra. Listen. Then you will tell it again, but as the crocodile.
flow.kid: Hear the story. Then you will be the crocodile.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tell It From the Other Side. You hear an old story, then tell it from another character's point of view.

flow.do: Ask your child to tell the story as the crocodile. They can start with 'I am a crocodile, and I live in the river.'
flow.say: Now you are the crocodile. What did you see from the water? Why did you go along with your wife? How did you feel when the monkey jumped back into the tree?
flow.kid: You are the crocodile. Tell the story. What did you want?

ask.q: What did the crocodile know that the monkey did not?
good: He knew his wife wanted the monkey's heart.
He knew it was a trick from the start.

flow.parent: The crocodile need not become a hero. The point is to see what the crocodile saw, knew and wanted, not to agree with him.

flow.do: Talk about what changed when the same story was told by the other side.
flow.say: Did the story change when the crocodile told it? Did anything in it change, or only the way we saw it?
flow.kid: Same story, two tellers. What changed?
flow.think: Think of a quarrel you had. How would the other person tell it?

activities.context: In this activity you tell an old Panchatantra story from the side of the crocodile instead of the monkey.

activities.title: Same and Different: a friend interview

materials.item: a friend, cousin or neighbour to interview, in person or on a phone call
paper and coloured pencils

activities.safety: Interview only people your family knows. A grown-up helps with a phone call.

schedule.what: Ask a friend six questions. Find three ways you are the same and three ways you are different.

activities.record: Draw two overlapping circles. Write what only you have in one, what only your friend has in the other, and what you share in the middle.

flow.do: Help your child write six questions, for example: Which hand do you write with? What is your favourite food? What scares you? What are you good at? What do you find hard? What do you do on a holiday?
flow.say: We are going to find out how you and your friend are the same and how you are different. What do you want to ask?
flow.kid: Write six questions for your friend.
flow.context: This is the first step of the friend interview. You find ways you and a friend are the same and different.

flow.do: Your child asks the questions and writes or draws the answers. They answer the questions themselves too.
flow.say: Ask each question, then listen to the whole answer before you say yours.
flow.kid: Ask a question. Listen to the whole answer. Then answer it yourself.
flow.parent: Listening without jumping in is the real skill here. A grown-up stays near for a phone call.

flow.do: Draw the two circles and fill them in. Talk about the answers.
flow.say: Did any answer surprise you? Is there something your friend finds easy that you find hard?
flow.kid: Fill in the circles. What surprised you?
flow.think: Could you be good friends with someone who is different in every circle?

projects.title: A Two-Sided Skit: one story, two points of view

materials.item: a story the child knows, such as Meenu and the monster, or the monkey and the crocodile
old dupattas, towels, paper and string for simple costumes
a phone to record the skit, held by a grown-up

projects.safety: A grown-up helps with scissors and handles the phone.

schedule.what: Choose a story. Plan two short scenes: the story as one character sees it, then the same events as the other character sees them. Make simple costumes.
Practise and act both scenes for the family. Record them and talk about what changed.

projects.record: Write the two scene plans, and after the show write one thing the audience noticed about the second scene.

flow.do: 1. Choose a story with two characters who see things differently. 2. Plan scene 1: the story as the first character tells it. 3. Plan scene 2: the same events as the second character tells them. 4. Make costumes from old cloth.
flow.say: A skit with two sides. First, the story as Meenu sees it. Then the same story as Kombu sees it. What will be different in the second scene?
flow.kid: Plan two scenes. Same story. Two different tellers.
flow.parent: Keep each scene to about two minutes. The events must stay the same in both scenes. Only what each character sees, knows and feels changes.
flow.context: This is the first day of a 2-day project. You plan a skit that tells one story from two sides.

flow.do: 1. Practise both scenes twice. 2. Act them for the family. 3. Record them on the phone. 4. Ask the audience what changed between the scenes.
flow.say: Now the show. After both scenes, we'll ask the audience: what changed, and what stayed the same?
flow.kid: Act both scenes. Ask the audience: what changed?
flow.think: Which scene did the audience feel was the true one?

projects.context: In this 2-day project you act one story twice, from two characters' points of view.

challenges.title: A Board Game Everyone Can Play
challenges.problem: Many board games use only colours to tell the players' pieces apart. A child with red-green colour blindness may not be able to tell red from green pieces. Make a simple race game that every child can play, whatever colours they see.
constraints: Use paper, bottle caps and things from home.
Each player's pieces must be easy to tell apart without using colour at all.
The game must work for at least three players.
materials: a sheet of paper or card for the board
bottle caps, buttons or folded paper for the pieces
a dice, or six slips of paper numbered 1 to 6
general: Give each player's pieces a different shape: a circle, a square, a triangle.
Draw a pattern on each player's pieces, such as stripes, dots or a star, as well as a colour.
Write a letter or number on each piece.
creative: Make pieces that feel different too, such as a smooth cap, a rough paper ball and a button, so a child who cannot see well can play by touch.
Mark special squares with both a colour and a picture, such as a ladder or a snake.
Test your board by looking at it through a colour blindness simulator on a phone, with a grown-up.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own race game. Ask someone else to play it and tell you if anything was hard to tell apart.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at a game at home and ask what would be hard for a colour-blind player.
flow.say: Imagine red and green look almost the same to you. Which games at home would be hard to play?
flow.kid: Red and green look the same. Which games get hard?
flow.context: This is a design challenge. You make a board game that people who see colours differently can all play.

flow.do: Draw a race board of about 30 squares. Make pieces for three players that differ in shape or pattern, not only colour.
flow.say: Make the pieces so that someone could tell them apart in a black and white photo.
flow.kid: Make pieces you can tell apart without colour.
flow.parent: A good test is a black and white photo on the phone. If the pieces still look different, the design works.

flow.do: Play one round and check the design.
flow.say: Could everyone tell their piece apart? What would you change?
flow.kid: Play once. Could everyone find their piece?
flow.think: What other things at home use only colour to tell you something?

challenges.title: The Fair Turns Plan: one swing, three children
challenges.problem: In a block of flats, three children want the one swing in the play area at the same time every evening. One is five, one is eight and one is ten. Design a turns plan that all three would call fair.
constraints: The plan must work without a grown-up watching all the time.
Each child must agree it is fair, from their own point of view.
It must be simple enough for a five-year-old to follow.
materials: three people to play the three children
general: Take turns of the same length, timed by counting swings, for example 20 swings each.
Go in order of who arrived first.
Take turns by age, youngest first.
creative: Let the youngest choose to be pushed, and count that turn as shorter.
Make a waiting game for the queue, so waiting is fun too.
Agree a special signal that means 'your turn is over' that nobody minds.
challenges.your_turn: Now make a fair turns plan for something your family shares: the TV remote, the window seat, or the last dosa.

flow.do: Each person plays one of the three children and says what they want and why.
flow.say: You are the five-year-old. What do you want? Now you are the ten-year-old. What do you want?
flow.kid: Be each child in turn. What do they want? Why?
flow.context: This is a design challenge. You make a plan for sharing one swing that three different children all call fair.

flow.do: Write a plan. Test it by playing it out with the three people.
flow.say: Will the five-year-old understand this plan? Will the ten-year-old think it is fair?
flow.kid: Write the plan. Act it out. Is it fair to all three?
flow.parent: There is no single right answer. A good plan names what each child needs. Counting swings works better than minutes for younger children.

flow.do: Talk about what made the plan fair or unfair.
flow.say: Is fair the same as equal? When might a different turn be fairer?
flow.kid: Is fair the same as everyone the same? Why?
