quiz.p: Kavya sits on one side of a table. A tall tumbler hides a lime from her. Can her mother, sitting on the other side, see the lime?
opts: Yes, if nothing is between her and the lime
No, because Kavya can't see it
Only if Kavya points at it
quiz.why: What one person can see depends on where they sit. The tumbler blocks Kavya's view, not her mother's. Picking 'No, because Kavya can't see it' means thinking everyone sees what you see.

quiz.p: Arjun faces his sister across a table. The banana is on Arjun's left. Where is it for his sister?
quiz.why: When two people face each other, left and right swap. If you chose 'on her left', stand face to face with someone and both point to one thing.

quiz.p: Nila puts her ball in the cupboard and goes out. Her brother moves the ball under the bed. Where will Nila look first when she comes back?
quiz.why: Nila did not see the ball being moved, so she still believes it is in the cupboard. Picking 'under the bed' is the answer most three-year-olds give: they mix up what is true with what Nila knows.

quiz.p: Why do two people sometimes believe different things about the same box?
opts: One of them is not clever
They have seen or been told different things
quiz.why: A belief comes from what a person has seen and heard. If one person saw inside and one did not, they can believe different things. Being clever has nothing to do with it.

quiz.p: In the Dominant Eye Test, what does 'dominant eye' mean?
opts: The stronger eye, which sees more clearly
The eye your brain uses first to aim and line things up
The eye on the same side as your writing hand
quiz.why: The dominant eye is the one the brain uses first for aiming. It is not always the clearer eye, and it is not always on the side of the writing hand.

quiz.p: About how many people in 10 write with their left hand?
quiz.why: About 1 person in 10 is left-handed. So in a class of 30 you might find about 3 left-handed children.

quiz.p: Meenakshi has red-green colour blindness. Which game piece would be easiest for her to tell apart from a green piece?
opts: A red piece with a star drawn on it
quiz.why: Red and green can look alike to her, but a star is a shape she can see clearly. Good designs use shape or pattern as well as colour.

quiz.p: Before Martin Hughes's hiding game in 1975, what did many people think about children under seven?
opts: They could not picture what another person sees
They could not play hiding games
They could see more than grown-ups
quiz.why: Jean Piaget and Bärbel Inhelder's three mountains task suggested young children saw only their own view. Hughes's game, which made sense to children, showed most children of three and four could do it.

quiz.p: In Hughes's game, children hid a boy doll from policeman dolls behind walls. What did most children aged three and four do?
opts: Hid the boy where the policemen could see him
Hid the boy where neither policeman could see him
quiz.why: About 9 children in 10 hid the doll in the right place. The task made sense to them, so they showed what they could really do.

quiz.p: In the Panchatantra story, the crocodile tells it his way. What changes?
opts: What the teller saw, knew and wanted
quiz.why: The same things happen, but each teller notices and explains them from their own place. If you chose 'the ending', remember the monkey still escapes.

quiz.p: Three children of different ages share one swing. What makes a turns plan fair?
opts: Each child can see why it is fair from their own point of view
quiz.why: A plan is fair when each person can see why it is fair from where they stand. 'The oldest decides' works for the oldest only.

quiz.p: In the Jigsaw Nimbu Paani activity, why did the family need everyone's card?
opts: Each card held a different part of the recipe
The cards were all the same
quiz.why: Each person held one part, so the drink could only be made together. This is the idea of the jigsaw classroom.

items.p: Divya sits opposite her father at a table. A tall steel dabba stands between them, with an onion right behind it on her father's side. Who can see the onion?
items.why: The dabba blocks Divya's view of the onion. Her father has nothing in his way. If you chose 'both', try it with a real dabba.

items.p: Two people sitting in different chairs at one table can both draw true pictures of it, even if the pictures are different.
items.why: True. Each drawing shows the table from one place. Both are true views of the same table.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the place someone sees from, or how they think about something
what a person thinks is true
a belief that is wrong because the person missed what changed
working together to reach a goal
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit.

items.p: Knowing that other people have their own thoughts, wishes and beliefs is called theory of ____.
items.why: Theory of mind means understanding that other people's minds hold different things from yours.

items.p: Sort these. Can you see it from outside, or is it hidden inside a person?
items.a: see items
items.why: Many differences between people cannot be seen. You find them out by testing, watching or asking.

items.p: Anjali closes her right eye and the clock stays in the paper hole. Which is her dominant eye?
items.why: With the right eye closed, only the left eye was looking, and the clock stayed in the hole. So she lines things up with her left eye.

items.p: Your dominant eye is always on the same side as the hand you write with.
items.why: False. For many people they match, but for many they do not. The Dominant Eye Test can show this in one family.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? A false belief, a mistake in a sum, a magic trick watcher, a surprise party guest.
items.why: The trick watcher and the party guest both believe something false because of what they have not seen. That is what a false belief is. A mistake in a sum comes from adding wrongly, not from missing what happened.

items.p: Farhan builds a cross of two books on the table, making four corners. A toy watchman stands at the end of one book. How many corners can the watchman see?
items.why: From the end of one wall, the watchman can look along both sides of it, into two corners. The other book hides the other two corners.

items.p: Put these steps of the Biscuit Box Surprise in order.
items: Fill a biscuit box with pencils
a: Fill a biscuit box with pencils
items.why: You need to guess before you ask, or the guess is not a real prediction.

items.p: Draw a tumbler and a banana on a table as you see them. Then draw them as someone on the other side of the table would see them.
items.a: Two drawings. In the second, the banana is on the other side of the tumbler, and anything hidden in the first may now be in view.
items.why: A strong answer swaps left and right in the second drawing, and shows what the tumbler hides from each side.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled 'From my chair' and 'From the other chair'.

items.p: Why could Meenu not see what Kombu needed, even after she lay on the floor next to him?
items.a: Lying on the floor showed her what Kombu could see, but not what he wanted or felt. She had to ask him.
items.why: A strong answer says that seeing from someone's place shows what they see, but feelings and needs must be told or asked about.

items.p: Kavya and her grandmother Lakshmi disagree about a quarrel between Kavya and her friend.

views.says: My friend took my pencil without asking, so she was wrong. I don't need to hear her side.
Before you decide, ask her why she took it. She may have seen or known something you did not.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example that the friend might have thought it was her pencil, or that taking without asking is still not fair. It also says what the other side has right: Kavya is right that asking first matters, and Lakshmi is right that the friend's view may change the story.
items.why: Both have a point. Hearing the other side does not mean the other side is right, but it may change what you think happened.

items.p: Kombu thought Meenu was scary, and Meenu thought Kombu was scary. Write why each one felt that way, using what each could see.
items.a: Meenu saw big horn shadows on the wall from her cot. Kombu, on the floor, saw a huge girl and heard a voice like thunder.
items.why: A strong answer links each fear to what each one could see or hear from their own place.

items.p: A psychologist gave each child in a group one part of a lesson, so they needed each other. What did his studies find?
opts: The children came to like each other more
items.why: Elliot Aronson's jigsaw classroom studies found children in these groups came to like each other more. Scientists still argue about when working together helps most.

items.p: Lakshmi sits at the side of a table, between Kavya and her mother. Which seat gives the hardest drawing to guess for Kavya?
items.why: From the side, things line up in a new way: one can now be in front of another. Many children find the side view hardest. Your own result may differ.

items.p: In the Other Chair Test, Kavya drew the lime, but put the banana on the wrong side. What does this tell you about the two steps of seeing from someone's place?
items.a: She knew what her mother could see, which is the first step. She got how it looked wrong, which is the second, harder step.
items.why: A strong answer separates knowing whether something is in view from knowing how it looks from there, including left and right.

items.p: Children of three usually know that a toy behind a wall is hidden from someone on the other side.
items.why: True. Even young children can tell what is in someone's view. Working out exactly how it looks from there comes later.

items.p: Sort these. Is the person's belief true or false?
items: Paati thinks the biscuit box holds biscuits, but it holds pencils
Arjun thinks his chappals are by the door, and they are
Maxi thinks his chocolate is in the cupboard, after his mother moved it
Divya thinks it is raining, and she can hear it on the roof
items.a: see items
items.why: A belief is false when the world changed or was different, and the person did not see or hear it.

items.p: A three-year-old sees the biscuit box opened to show pencils. Many three-year-olds then say something surprising. What?
opts: That they knew it held pencils all along
items.why: Many children of three say they thought 'pencils' from the start, and that the next person will say 'pencils' too. They find it hard to hold what they used to believe apart from what they now know.

items.p: Why did scientists need a story with a false belief, like Maxi and the chocolate, to test theory of mind? Why not just ask where the chocolate is?
items.a: If Maxi's belief were true, a child could answer by saying where the chocolate really is. Only a false belief shows whether the child understands what Maxi thinks.
items.why: A strong answer says the right answer must be different from the truth, so we can tell whether the child is thinking about Maxi's mind or about the real world.

items.p: In the Dominant Eye Test, Paati's eye changed from try to try. What is the best thing to write?
opts: Right, because most people are right-eyed
Not clear, and test again another day
Left, because her first try was left
items.why: Some people do not have a clear dominant eye. A scientist writes what they really found, not what is usual.

items.p: A family of 6 did the Dominant Eye Test. 4 were right-eyed and 2 were left-eyed. 5 wrote with their right hand. How many people at least must have had a dominant eye on a different side from their writing hand?
items.why: 5 are right-handed, but only 4 are right-eyed. So at least 1 right-handed person must be left-eyed.

items.p: When two people face each other, their left and right are ____.
items.why: Your right hand is on the same side of the table as their left hand.

items.p: Studies find that friends are more likely than other children to talk a quarrel through and stay together after it.
items.why: True. Friends quarrel too, but they are more likely to sort it out. Understanding each other's point of view helps.

items.p: Draw your room the way an ant on the floor would see the room. Then write one thing the ant can see that you never notice.
items.a: A drawing from very low down: huge table legs, chappals, the underside of the bed. One noticed thing, such as dust or a crumb under the cupboard.
items.why: A strong answer draws from the floor and notices what a small being on the floor needs or meets.

items.p: Chimpanzee scientists hid one piece of food from a high-ranking chimp with a screen. Which piece did the low-ranking chimp mostly take?
opts: The piece the high-ranking chimp could see
The piece hidden from the high-ranking chimp
items.why: The low-ranking chimp mostly took the hidden piece. Many scientists think this shows the chimp knew what the other could see. Others think a simple rule could explain it.

items.p: Two scientists disagree about the chimpanzee food test.

views.says: The low-ranking chimp knew what the high-ranking chimp could see, and chose the hidden food for that reason.
The chimp may follow a rule, such as 'go for food behind a screen', without thinking about what the other chimp sees.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? What test could you design to tell the two ideas apart?
items.a: A strong answer picks one side with a reason, and suggests a test where the two ideas predict different things, for example a see-through screen, where the rule says go but the other chimp can see.
items.why: Good science designs a test where two ideas give different answers.

items.p: In Jigsaw Nimbu Paani, what would have happened if the youngest person had refused to read their card?
items.a: The drink could not be made properly, because one step would be missing.
items.why: A strong answer says every card was needed, so every person mattered, whatever their age.

items.p: On the drawing of a cross of two books seen from above, label each corner with the watchmen who can see it: A, B, both or neither.
items.a: The two corners each watchman looks into are labelled with that watchman; the corner both see is labelled both; the one corner neither sees is labelled neither.
items.why: From the end of a wall, a watchman sees the two corners beside it. With two watchmen at the ends of two walls next to each other, one corner is seen by both, and one by neither.
items.art: A plus-shaped cross of two books seen from above, with watchman A at the end of the top book and watchman B at the end of the right book, and four blank labels in the corners.

items.p: Jean Piaget and Bärbel Inhelder's three mountains task asked children to choose a picture of what a doll saw. Why might this be harder than hiding a toy from a watchman, even if a child can picture the doll's view?
items.a: Choosing between photos of mountains is a strange and hard job for a small child. Hiding from a watchman is a game that makes sense, and the child can check by looking.
items.why: A strong answer says a test can fail because the task is confusing, not because the child cannot take another view.

items.p: Martin Hughes's game showed that most young children can work out what another sees. What does this teach about testing?
opts: A test can show less than a person can do, if it does not make sense to them
items.why: Piaget's idea came from a task that confused young children. A task that made sense showed more. Piaget was right about many other things.

items.p: Two friends disagree about choosing friends.

views.says: It is best to be friends with people just like you. You like the same games, so you never fight.
It is best to have friends who are different. They know things you don't and can help with what you find hard.
Most children choose friends who are like them, but friends with different skills can help each other a lot.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give a reason from your own life. Then say what the other side has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason and an example, and admits what the other side gets right: similar friends do find it easy to play, and different friends do bring new skills.
items.why: Both are true for different friendships. The evidence says similar friends are common, not that different friends are worse.

items.p: Many people think 'If I can't see it, nobody can.' Describe a test you could do at home to show this is wrong.
items.a: Hide a thing behind a tumbler from yourself, then take a photo from the other side, or ask someone there what they see.
items.why: A strong answer describes a test with a hidden thing and a way to check another person's view, such as a photo or going to their seat.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Writing hand, dominant eye, height, colour vision.
items.why: You can see someone's height just by looking. Their writing hand, dominant eye and colour vision you find out only by watching or testing them.

items.p: In many countries about 1 boy in 12 has red-green colour blindness, but only about 1 girl in 200. In a school of 600 boys and 600 girls, about how many would you expect to be colour blind?
items.why: 600 divided by 12 is 50 boys. 600 divided by 200 is 3 girls. 50 + 3 = 53. The real number in any one school may be different.

items.p: If two people look at the same chilli, they always receive the same picture of it.
items.why: False. A person with colour blindness may see the colours differently, and someone in a different place sees a different side.

items.p: Wimmer and Perner's Maxi test asks where Maxi will look. Make up a new story, set in your home, that tests the same idea.
items.a: A strong story has a person who puts something somewhere and leaves, someone who moves it, and the question of where the first person will look.
items.why: A good test must have a false belief, so the right answer is different from where the thing really is.

items.p: Draw a picture plan of a shared space in a block of flats, such as the play area, that works for a child in a wheelchair, a grandmother and a toddler.
items.a: A plan with a ramp, benches in the shade, a low fence round a toddler area and wide paths.
items.why: A strong answer thinks from each person's place and gives each one something they need.

items.p: The jigsaw classroom gave each child one part of a lesson. Why might this help children who did not get on to like each other?
opts: They had to listen to each other to learn
They were told to be kind
items.why: Each child needed the others' parts, so listening and helping were useful. Being told to be kind is less likely to change how children feel.

items.p: Gordon Allport said meeting people from another group helps most when people are equals and share a goal. Why might meeting while competing make things worse?
items.a: When people compete, the other side becomes someone to beat, so they may get on worse.
items.why: A strong answer links the result to what each side wants: a shared goal makes the other side useful, a contest makes them a rival.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found.
pairs: most children of three and four can hide a doll from a policeman doll
children of about five understand that Maxi will look in the wrong place
children in jigsaw groups came to like each other more
a low-ranking chimp took food a high-ranking chimp could not see
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these tests looked at how one mind works out what another sees, knows or needs.

items.p: Label the drawing of a table seen from above: mark where to sit to see the lime, where to sit so it is hidden, and draw a line from each seat's eyes to the lime.
items.a: The seat on the lime's side is labelled 'sees the lime'. The seat behind the tumbler is labelled 'hidden'. Its line to the lime passes through the tumbler.
items.why: Light travels in straight lines, so a line from the eye that passes through the tumbler means the lime is hidden from that seat.
items.art: A table from above with a tumbler, a lime close behind it and four empty seats round the table.

items.p: The Jain idea that every view sees only part of the truth is called ____.
items.why: Anekantavada means many-sidedness. The story of the blind men and the elephant is about this idea.

items.p: Hearing the other person's side of a quarrel means you must agree with them.
items.why: False. Hearing their side tells you what they saw and wanted. You can still disagree, but now you disagree about what really happened.

applications: Map makers and app designers test their maps with colour-blind users, and use shapes and labels as well as colours.
Architects design ramps, rails and wide doors by thinking from the place of someone in a wheelchair or with a pram.
Teachers use group work like the jigsaw classroom, so children from different backgrounds learn to work together.
Doctors and nurses learn to explain an illness from the patient's point of view, not only their own.
Cricket fielders and goalkeepers guess where a ball will go by picturing what the batter or kicker sees.

spotted.text: The mirrors on an auto-rickshaw or a bus, which let the driver see what is behind, from where they sit.
spotted.art: An auto-rickshaw's side mirror showing a scooter behind it.

spotted.text: Railway platform signs in several languages, so people from different places can all read them.
spotted.art: A railway station sign in Tamil, Hindi and English.

spotted.text: A ramp next to the steps at a temple, a hospital or a metro station.
spotted.art: A ramp with a rail beside a short flight of steps at a metro station entrance.

spotted.text: Traffic lights with the red always at the top and green at the bottom, so people who see colours differently can go by position.
spotted.art: A traffic light on a busy Indian road, with the red light at the top.

open_questions.q: How does the brain build a picture of what another person is thinking?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found brain areas that are busy when we think about other minds, but nobody knows how they do it.

open_questions.q: Do any animals understand false beliefs, the way a five-year-old does?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies with apes that watched a video and looked where a person would wrongly search suggest they might. Others say the results can be explained more simply. The tests are still being argued over.

open_questions.q: Why do some people find it much easier than others to see from another person's point of view?
open_questions.why_open: Genes, upbringing, practice and the language a family speaks may all play a part. How much each matters is not known.

ask_kids: From where you are sitting now, what can I see that you can't?
What do you think the crow at the window thinks of our balcony?
If your little cousin came to visit, what would look big and scary to them in our flat?
Think of a quarrel today. How would the other person tell it?
Which hand does each person at this meal eat with? Is anyone different?
What does Paati know about our street that we don't?

jokes.j: Why did the tumbler hide the lime?
jokes.a: It wanted to see things from the lime's point of view.

jokes.j: What did the left hand say to the right hand across the table?
jokes.a: From where I sit, you're the one on the wrong side.

jokes.j: Why did the crocodile tell the story differently?
jokes.a: He saw it from the river bed.

jokes.j: What did the biscuit box say when Paati opened it?
jokes.a: Surprise! I'm full of pencils, not biscuits.

jokes.j: Why did the watchman never find the toy?
jokes.a: He kept looking at things from his own point of view.

jokes.j: What do you call two friends who share one umbrella?
Why did the ant think the chappal was a building?
jokes.a: Because from the floor, everything is sky-high.

jokes.j: How many eyes do you need to look through a keyhole?
jokes.a: Just one, and your brain already picked it.

jokes.j: Why did the friend sit in the other chair?
jokes.a: To see the lime that the tumbler was hiding from him.

jokes.j: What did the crow at the window say about the family at breakfast?
jokes.a: From up here, all I see is the dosa.

jokes.j: Why was the left-handed girl always happy at the table?
jokes.a: Because she always had her right on her side.

jokes.j: Why did Kombu the monster ask for idli?
jokes.a: Because it is soft on horns and easy on claws.

maths.problem: In the Other Chair Test, Kavya made 3 drawings of other seats. In each one she checked 4 things: the lime, the banana's side, the tumbler, and what was in front. She got 9 things right in all. What fraction of her checks were right?
maths.answer: 9 out of 12, which is three quarters.
maths.explain: 3 drawings with 4 checks each is 3 times 4, which is 12 checks. She got 9 right. 9 out of 12 is the same as 3 out of 4, which is three quarters.
maths.context: This is about the Other Chair Test, where you draw what someone in another chair sees.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets you compare your score with someone who made a different number of drawings.

maths.problem: Arjun's family did the Dominant Eye Test. Appa, Amma and Paati are right-eyed. Arjun and his sister are left-eyed. Draw a tally and a bar chart. Is the result surprising, if about 2 people in 3 are right-eyed?
maths.answer: 3 right-eyed and 2 left-eyed. It is not very surprising: in a small group, the numbers can easily differ from the usual 2 in 3.
maths.explain: With 5 people, 2 in 3 would be a little more than 3 right-eyed. 3 right-eyed is close. A small group often differs from the pattern in a big group.
maths.context: This is about the Dominant Eye Test, where each person finds the eye they aim with.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows the family's result at a glance, and comparing it with the usual pattern shows why small groups can be misleading.

maths.problem: Three children share one swing. Each turn is 20 swings, and one swing takes about 3 seconds. How long does one child wait while the other two have their turns?
maths.explain: Two turns of 20 swings is 40 swings. 40 times 3 seconds is 120 seconds, which is 2 minutes.
maths.context: This is about the Fair Turns Plan, where three children share one swing.
maths.why_maths: Working out the waiting time helps you judge whether a plan feels fair to the one who waits.

maths.problem: In the hiding game, two watchmen stand at the ends of two books that are next to each other. There are 4 corners. Watchman A sees 2 corners and watchman B sees 2 corners. Exactly 1 corner is seen by both. How many corners are hidden from both?
maths.explain: A and B see 2 + 2 = 4 corners, but 1 corner was counted twice. So together they see 3 different corners. 4 - 3 = 1 corner is hidden from both.
maths.context: This is about Hide From the Watchmen, where you hide a toy behind two crossed books.
maths.why_maths: Counting carefully, without counting a corner twice, tells you exactly how many hiding places there are before you try.

roots.context: We have drawn the table from other chairs, found hidden differences in our family, and played at being someone else. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: From your chair, the tumbler hid the lime. From the chair opposite, the lime was in plain view, and the banana sat on the other side. Each true view left out something another view showed. So you learn the whole table only by putting views together.
deep_truth.habit: We take what we see from our own place to be the way things are. But every view comes from one place, and every place has something hidden behind something else.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Other Chair Test, the photo from each seat showed something the others did not: the hidden lime, the banana's side, what stood in front.

three.who_am_i: You are a viewer in one place at a time, and other people are viewers too, each in their own place.
three.what_is_life: Every living being, an ant on the floor or a crow at the window, meets the world from where they are, with their own senses and needs.
three.what_is_this_world: The world has more sides than any one person can see at once.

roots.thread: One table sits in the middle of the room. Every chair round it gets a different picture of that one table, and each picture is true. Every person, crow and ant in the house is another such place, looking out. The many views do not split the world into pieces. Put together, they show more of the one world than any single view can.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, a Buddhist text, and the Jain teaching of anekantavada
teachings.teaching: A king asks some blind men to touch an elephant. One touches the trunk and says an elephant is like a pipe. One touches the ear and says it is like a fan. One touches the leg and says it is like a pillar. They quarrel, each sure he is right. The Jains call the lesson anekantavada, many-sidedness: each view holds part of the truth.
teachings.link: In the Other Chair Test, each drawing was right about what that chair could see, and none showed the whole table. Like the elephant, the table was known only by putting the views together.

teachings.teaching: As a hand moves at once to catch a slipping garment, a true friend moves at once to remove a friend's trouble.
teachings.link: To help in time, a friend must notice the trouble, which means seeing from the other person's place, the way Meenu learned to see from Kombu's.

science.text: Most children understand that another person can see what they cannot by about three, and that another person can believe something false by about five.
How the brain builds its picture of another person's mind is not known.

other_view.who: Protagoras, a Greek thinker about 2,400 years ago, as Plato reported him
other_view.view: Each person is the measure of things. What seems true to you is true for you, and what seems true to me is true for me. On this view there is no one whole to find by putting views together, only many views.

practice.title: Sit in someone else's place
practice.say: Today at a meal, swap seats with someone in the family. Sit still in their seat for one minute and just look. Breathe slowly three times. What can you see from here that you never see from your own chair? Tell each other one thing.
practice.kid: Sit in someone else's chair. Look for one minute. Breathe slowly. What can you see from here? Tell them.

ask: If every seat shows a different true table, is there a table that nobody is looking at?
Can you ever fully know what another person sees and feels, or only come close?
If an ant, a crow and you each see the balcony differently, whose balcony is it?
roots.art: A family sitting round a dining table, each person with a faint picture above their head showing the tumbler, banana and lime from their own seat.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat. Choices made: the Other Chair Test uses a tall steel tumbler and a lime pressed against it, so the lime is fully hidden from one seat; a photo from the other seat at sitting eye height is the check, and with no phone the child goes and sits there. The Dominant Eye Test uses a postcard with a hole and a wall clock 3 metres away; some people get different eyes on different tries, so the steps say to write 'not clear'. The hiding game uses two books crossed in a plus; with watchmen at the ends of two neighbouring books, exactly one corner is hidden from both. The Biscuit Box Surprise will very likely show grown-ups saying 'biscuits', which the child predicts: the surprising answers come only from children of three or four, so that part is optional and needs their family's agreement. Nimbu paani needs a grown-up to cut the lime. The Panchatantra story is told from memory. The spine is the intro, the hiding game, the Other Chair Test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1940s in Geneva, Jean Piaget and Bärbel Inhelder made a model of three mountains. A child sat on one side, and a doll was put on another. The child was asked to choose, from a set of pictures, the one showing what the doll could see. Many children under about seven chose the picture of their own view. Piaget and Inhelder decided that young children cannot picture another person's view. They called this egocentrism. In 1975, Martin Hughes, working in Edinburgh, tried a game that made more sense to children. He crossed two walls to make four spaces, and placed two policeman dolls looking for a boy doll. Children of three and four had to hide the boy where neither policeman could see him. About nine in ten did it right. The psychologist Margaret Donaldson made this study famous in her book Children's Minds in 1978. She argued that the mountains task was hard because it did not make human sense to a small child, not because the child could not see from another place.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean Piaget and Bärbel Inhelder in Geneva, Martin Hughes and Margaret Donaldson in Edinburgh
how_we_found_out.when: 1940s (the three mountains task) and 1975 (Hughes's policeman doll game)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Piaget and Inhelder thought children under about seven could not picture what someone else sees. Hughes's hiding game, which made sense to children, showed that most children of three and four could.
